question: Which statement best describes What ISR actually does?
options: Exporting a revalidate value from a route segment sets the regeneration window for the whole route, regardless of individual fetch options. This is the cleanest way to declare 'this page is ISR with an N-second window' for an entire page.

ISR serves a pre-built static page (like SSG) but attaches a revalidate time to it. After that window elapses, the next request still gets the cached page instantly, while Next regenerates a fresh version in the background; subsequent requests get the updated page. You keep CDN-fast delivery and gain periodic freshness without redeploying.

You can set the refresh window on an individual fetch via its next.revalidate option, which makes that data (and the route depending on it) regenerate after the given number of seconds. Different fetches can have different windows; the route's effective revalidate is the smallest of them.

Instead of waiting for the timer, you can invalidate cached pages the moment data changes — call revalidatePath('/products') or revalidateTag('products') from a Server Action, route handler, or webhook. Pages then regenerate on the next request, so content updates instantly when a CMS or backend changes.

question: Which statement best describes Route segment revalidate?
options: Exporting a revalidate value from a route segment sets the regeneration window for the whole route, regardless of individual fetch options. This is the cleanest way to declare 'this page is ISR with an N-second window' for an entire page.

ISR wins when content is public and benefits from static speed/SEO but changes too often to rebuild the whole site each time, and a small staleness window is acceptable. It beats pure SSG (which is frozen until redeploy) on freshness, and beats SSR (per-request render) on speed and cost for cacheable content.
